questions.stem: In public the senator {1} the practice of torture in terms that admitted no exception; his voting record, however, revealed at most a mild {2}, one he set aside whenever intelligence officials pressed him to authorize it.
questions.explanation: The semicolon and "however" set absolute public condemnation against a feeling weak enough to be dropped on request, so blank one needs the top of the hatred scale — abhorred, the verb of moral line-drawing about a practice. Countenanced and relished would leave nothing for the contrast to work against. In blank two only aversion is a feeling one could "set aside" in order to authorize torture; a penchant or affinity would be a liking for it, which reverses the sentence.

questions.stem: Whatever his failings as a politician, Adams genuinely {1} the traffic in human beings, and spent his last years in Congress fighting it at the cost of every alliance he had.
questions.explanation: Abhorred and loathed are the two that yield the same sentence: deep disgust at a practice, consistent with a career spent fighting it. Countenanced and tolerated form a tempting equivalent pair of their own, and relished and cherished another, but both pairs are killed by the clause about fighting the traffic at ruinous personal cost.

questions.stem: By the third hour the college's victory celebration had grown so {1} that the porters, who had watched a century of such nights, propped the gates open and waited it out with folded arms.
questions.explanation: Only boisterous describes noisy, physical high spirits — the surplus energy of people enjoying themselves, which the porters indulge rather than suppress. Obdurate and obstinate mean unyielding, obsequious means fawning, and none of the three is a property of a sound or a crowd's exuberance; placid reverses the sentence, since a calm celebration would need no waiting out.

questions.stem: Promised an easy November passage, the emigrants spent three days pinned to their bunks while the {1} Atlantic sent crockery sliding the length of the galley.
questions.explanation: Of wind and sea, boisterous carries its older sense of rough and wild, making it equivalent here to turbulent. Placid and halcyon form a plausible pair but contradict the flying crockery; cacophonous concerns discordant sound and obstreperous concerns noisy defiance of control, neither of which is a way for an ocean to behave.

questions.stem: Offered the seat with a flourish she found more theatrical than {1}, she took it anyway: to refuse a courtesy that had plainly cost the man something, however dated its style, would have been {2}.
questions.explanation: Blank one contrasts empty display with the genuine article — self-sacrificing, faintly archaic gallantry — which is chivalrous; obsequious would make the gesture self-serving flattery rather than something that cost him, and boorish is not a standard anyone is falling short of. Blank two names the failure to rise to a kindness one has accepted the value of, which is precisely churlish; obstinate describes stubbornness and imprudent a miscalculation, neither of which is about ingratitude.

questions.stem: Scott's novels fixed the popular image of the Middle Ages as an age of {1} self-denial — the knight surrendering his horse, his cloak and his place in the line — though the chronicles record a good deal more plunder than protection.
questions.explanation: The examples are all acts of protective, honourable self-sacrifice performed under a code, which is what chivalrous means. Urbane describes polished social manner and implies no sacrifice, obsequious implies servility aimed at advantage, and boisterous and churlish are the wrong register entirely.

questions.stem: Given how promptly the foundation covered the museum's deficit, it would be {1} to dwell now on the conditions it attached to the gift.
questions.explanation: The frame is the concessive negative in which churlish lives — a sour, grudging response to a benefit already received — and ungracious says the same thing. Gauche means socially clumsy and brusque means curt in manner, faults of style rather than of gratitude; imprudent and impertinent both fit the grammar but change the complaint to unwisdom or presumption.

questions.stem: The innkeeper, who had prayed all winter for exactly this custom, found he could not resent the {1} crowd singing in his yard after the races: to grudge a man his noise when the man's money was already in the till would have been {2}.
questions.explanation: Blank one must name cheerful, loud, unresentable rowdiness — boisterous — since taciturn crowds make no noise to resent and obsequious describes fawning, not volume. Blank two turns on the innkeeper having already profited: complaining anyway would be the small, grudging meanness of spirit that churlish names, whereas chivalrous is praise and vociferous merely repeats the idea of loudness.
